CALIFORNIA GROCERY WORKER RETENTION LAW — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Grocery, Inc.

GROCERY WORKER RETENTION LAW — TRANSITION RECORD
CALIFORNIA GROCERY WORKER RETENTION LAW — TRANSITION RECORD

Successor grocery employer completing this record: Acme Grocery, Inc.
Incumbent grocery employer (owner/operator before the change in control): Old Owner Grocery Co.
Grocery establishment covered by this record: 123 Main St. store location
Date the transfer document effecting the change in control was executed: September 4, 2026
Approximate number of eligible grocery workers affected: 45

This record documents, as of the date signed below, Acme Grocery, Inc.'s actions with respect to the transition described above under California's grocery worker retention law, Labor Code §§ 2500-2522 (Division 2, Part 9.5, “Grocery Workers”).

WHO AND WHAT THE LAW COVERS
California's grocery worker retention law applies only within a specific set of defined terms found in Labor Code § 2502. A “grocery establishment” is limited to a retail store located in California that is over 15,000 square feet in size and that sells primarily household foodstuffs for offsite consumption — including fresh produce, meats, poultry, fish, deli products, dairy products, canned and dry foods, beverages, and baked or prepared foods — with any other merchandise being secondary to that primary food-sales purpose; a store that has ceased operating for 12 months or more falls outside the definition, while a distribution center a grocery establishment owns and operates mainly to supply its own stores counts as a grocery establishment regardless of its square footage. The triggering event is a “change in control”: a sale, purchase, assignment, acquisition, transfer, contribution, or other disposition of all or substantially all of the assets, cash on hand, or a controlling interest of the incumbent grocery employer, including through a merger, consolidation, or reorganization — not simply any change in day-to-day management or personnel. The employer that owned, controlled, or operated the grocery establishment before that event is the law's “incumbent grocery employer”; the one that owns, controls, or operates it afterward is the “successor grocery employer,” which the statute notes may in fact be the same entity as the incumbent employer when a change in control occurs without a change in the employer of record. Only certain workers qualify for the law's protections: an “eligible grocery worker” is an individual whose primary place of employment is the covered establishment and who worked for the incumbent grocery employer for at least six months before the transfer document was executed, and the definition expressly excludes managerial, supervisory, or confidential employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Change in control” means any sale, purchase, assignment, acquisition, transfer, contribution, or other disposition of all or substantially all of the assets, cash on hand, or a controlling interest, including by consolidation, merger, or reorganization, of or by the incumbent grocery employer or any person who controls the incumbent grocery employer or any grocery establishment under the operation or control of either the incumbent grocery employer or any person who controls the incumbent grocery employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2502(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, “change in control” definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2502.)
  "“Eligible grocery worker” means any individual whose primary place of employment is at the grocery establishment subject to a change in control, and who has worked for the incumbent grocery employer for at least six months prior to the execution of the transfer document. “Eligible grocery worker” does not include a managerial, supervisory, or confidential employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2502(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, “eligible grocery worker” definition and exclusions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2502.)
  "“Grocery establishment” means a retail store in this state that is over 15,000 square feet in size and that sells primarily household foodstuffs for offsite consumption, including the sale of fresh produce, meats, poultry, fish, deli products, dairy products, canned foods, dry foods, beverages, baked foods, or prepared foods. Other household supplies or other products shall be secondary to the primary purpose of food sales. A distribution center owned and operated by a grocery establishment and used primarily to distribute goods to or from its owned stores shall be considered a grocery establishment, regardless of its square footage. A grocery establishment does not include a retail store that has ceased operations for 12 months or more."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2502(d) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, “grocery establishment” definition and size threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2502.)
  "“Successor grocery employer” means the person that owns, controls, or operates the grocery establishment after the change in control. A successor grocery employer may be the same entity as an incumbent employer when a change in control occurs but the covered employer remains the same."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2502(h) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, “successor grocery employer” definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2502.)
  Known gap: All four quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 2502) rather than independently authored sources. This clause does not separately quote § 2502's definitions of “employment commencement date,” “job classification,” “person,” or “transfer document,” which are more mechanical and are used, where relevant, elsewhere in this document. This law (Lab. Code §§ 2500-2522) is a wholly separate statute from the Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act (Lab. Code §§ 1060-1065) covered elsewhere in this corpus: the janitor law is triggered by a change in an awarding authority's janitorial-services contract, while this law is triggered by a change in ownership or control of the grocery establishment itself, and the two statutes use different size thresholds, different retention periods (60 days under the janitor law versus 90 days here), and different defined terms.

INFORMATION TRANSFER AND POSTED PUBLIC NOTICE AFTER A CHANGE IN CONTROL
Once a covered change in control occurs, the law imposes information-sharing and posting duties that run separately from the retention obligation itself. Within 15 days after the transfer document is executed, the incumbent grocery employer must give the successor grocery employer and any collective bargaining representative the name, address, date of hire, and job classification of each eligible grocery worker, along with that worker's cellular telephone number and email address if known; if the incumbent grocery employer misses that 15-day deadline, the successor grocery employer may instead obtain the same information from a collective bargaining representative. Separately, the incumbent grocery employer must post public notice of the change in control at the affected grocery establishment within five business days after the transfer document is executed, and the notice must remain posted through any closure of the establishment and until it reopens as fully operational under the successor grocery employer. That posted notice must state the incumbent grocery employer's name and contact information, the successor grocery employer's name and contact information, and the effective date of the change in control, and it must be placed somewhere conspicuous where eligible grocery workers, other employees, customers, and the public can readily see it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The incumbent grocery employer shall, within 15 days after the execution of the transfer document, provide to the successor grocery employer and any collective bargaining representative the name, address, date of hire, employment occupation classification, and, if known, the cellular telephone number and email address of each eligible grocery worker."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2504(a)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, incumbent employer's 15-day employee-information transfer duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2504.)
  "If the incumbent grocery employer does not provide the information specified in paragraph (1) within 15 days, the successor grocery employer may obtain the information from a collective bargaining representative."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2504(a)(2) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, fallback to the collective bargaining representative (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2504.)
  "The incumbent grocery employer shall post public notice of the change in control at the location of the affected grocery establishment within five business days following the execution of the transfer document. Notice shall remain posted during any closure of the grocery establishment and until the grocery establishment is fully operational and open to the public under the successor grocery employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2508(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, posted public notice of a change in control (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2508.)
  "Notice shall include, but not be limited to, the name of the incumbent grocery employer and its contact information, the name of the successor grocery employer and its contact information, and the effective date of the change in control. (c) Notice shall be posted in a conspicuous place at the grocery establishment in a manner to be readily viewed by eligible grocery workers and other employees, customers, and members of the public."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2508(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, required content and conspicuous placement of the posted notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2508.)
  Known gap: The two § 2504(a) quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 2504) and are not independent of one another; the two § 2508 quotes are likewise subdivisions of a single, separate section (Labor Code § 2508) and are not independent of one another, though § 2504 and § 2508 are independently numbered sections relative to each other. This clause does not address § 2504(b)'s preferential-hiring-list requirement or § 2504(c)'s written-offer record-retention requirement, which are covered in a separate clause of this document.

THE PREFERENTIAL HIRING LIST AND THE 90-DAY RETENTION OBLIGATION
The law's central protection is a retention requirement built around a preferential hiring list. The successor grocery employer must maintain a preferential hiring list made up of the eligible grocery workers identified through the notice process, and must hire from that list for a period beginning when the transfer document is executed and continuing for 90 days after the grocery establishment reopens as fully operational under the successor grocery employer. Each eligible grocery worker the successor grocery employer hires under the law must then be retained for at least 90 days measured from that worker's own “employment commencement date” (the date the worker actually starts working for the successor grocery employer), during which the worker is employed on the terms and conditions the successor grocery employer sets, subject to any applicable collective bargaining agreement. If, during that hiring-list period, the successor grocery employer determines it needs fewer eligible grocery workers than the incumbent grocery employer required, it cannot pick and choose among them freely: workers within a job classification must be retained by seniority to the extent comparable classifications exist (or under the terms of a relevant collective bargaining agreement), and workers who are not classified must be retained by seniority and experience, or under the terms of a relevant collective bargaining agreement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The successor grocery employer shall maintain a preferential hiring list of eligible grocery workers identified by the incumbent grocery employer or collective bargaining representative pursuant to subdivision (a) and shall hire from that list for a period beginning upon the execution of the transfer document and continuing for 90 days after the grocery establishment is fully operational and open to the public under the successor grocery employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2504(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, preferential hiring list requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2504.)
  "A successor grocery employer shall retain each eligible grocery worker hired pursuant to this part for at least 90 days after the eligible grocery worker’s employment commencement date. During this 90-day transition employment period, eligible grocery workers shall be employed under the terms and conditions established by the successor grocery employer and pursuant to the terms of a relevant collective bargaining agreement, if any."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2506(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, 90-day retention requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2506.)
  "If, within the period established in subdivision (b) of Section 2504, the successor grocery employer determines that it requires fewer eligible grocery workers than were required by the incumbent grocery employer, the successor grocery employer shall retain eligible grocery workers by seniority within each job classification to the extent that comparable job classifications exist or pursuant to the terms of a relevant collective bargaining agreement, if any. Nonclassified eligible grocery workers shall be retained by seniority and according to experience or pursuant to the terms of a relevant collective bargaining agreement, if any."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2506(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, seniority-based retention when fewer workers are needed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2506.)
  Known gap: The § 2506(a) and § 2506(b) quotes below are both subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 2506) and are not independent of one another. The § 2504(b) quote is drawn from a separate, independently numbered section (Labor Code § 2504); § 2506(b) cross-references the hiring-list period defined in § 2504(b) by its own subdivision letter, so the two sections operate together even though they are not subdivisions of the same section.

DISCHARGE PROTECTION, THE END-OF-PERIOD EVALUATION, AND ANTI-RETALIATION
Retention under the law carries a job-security floor for as long as it lasts, plus a separate check-in point when it ends. During the 90-day transition employment period itself, the successor grocery employer may not discharge a retained eligible grocery worker without cause. At the end of that 90-day period, the successor grocery employer must give each retained eligible grocery worker a written performance evaluation and keep a copy of it for at least three years; if the worker's performance during the 90 days was satisfactory, the successor grocery employer must consider offering the worker continued employment on the terms and conditions the successor grocery employer sets and as otherwise required by law. Separately from the retention and evaluation mechanics, the law includes its own anti-retaliation provision: an employer may not refuse to employ, terminate, reduce the pay of, or otherwise take adverse action against an employee for seeking to enforce rights under the law, including by participating in a proceeding, opposing a practice the law prohibits, or otherwise asserting rights under it — and that protection extends to an employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges the law was not followed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "During the 90-day transition employment period, the successor grocery employer shall not discharge without cause an eligible grocery worker retained pursuant to this part."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2506(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, no discharge without cause during the transition period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2506.)
  "At the end of the 90-day transition employment period, the successor grocery employer shall make a written performance evaluation for each eligible grocery worker retained pursuant to this part. If the eligible grocery worker’s performance during the 90-day transition employment period is satisfactory, the successor grocery employer shall consider offering the eligible grocery worker continued employment under the terms and conditions established by the successor grocery employer and as required by law. The successor grocery employer shall retain a record of the written performance evaluation for at least three years."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2506(d) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, end-of-period written evaluation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2506.)
  "An employer shall not refuse to employ, terminate, reduce the compensation of, or otherwise take adverse action against any employee for seeking to enforce their rights under this part, including participating in proceedings, opposing any practice prescribed by this part, or otherwise asserting rights under this part. This section applies to an employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges noncompliance with this part."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2509 (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, anti-retaliation provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2509.)
  Known gap: The § 2506(c) and § 2506(d) quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 2506) and are not independent of one another. The § 2509 quote is drawn from a separate, independently numbered section (Labor Code § 2509). Note for anyone comparing this to the Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act covered elsewhere in this corpus: that statute expressly states that employment after its transition period becomes ordinary at-will employment (Lab. Code § 1061(f)). This grocery worker law does not contain equivalent language — § 2506(d) requires only that the successor grocery employer “consider offering” continued employment after a satisfactory 90-day evaluation, and this document did not locate, and does not assume, any provision in §§ 2500-2522 that independently classifies the legal status of employment after the 90-day period ends.

SMALL-EMPLOYER EXEMPTION, BARGAINING OUT, AND HOW THE LAW IS ENFORCED
The law's reach has specific limits, and its enforcement runs through both a private right of action and the Labor Commissioner. It does not apply to a change in control where the incumbent and successor grocery employers' combined nationwide grocery-worker headcounts, counted immediately before the change in control, total fewer than 300 — a small-employer exemption that reuses the statute's own “grocery establishment” definition but expands it to include out-of-state stores for purposes of that headcount. Parties covered by the law may also bargain out of some or all of its requirements: a collective bargaining agreement can supersede the law's requirements, but only if the agreement says so explicitly, in clear and unambiguous terms identifying which requirements it replaces. As for enforcement, an aggrieved employee or an employee representative (such as a union or a nonprofit corporation) may sue in superior court for violations and may recover hiring and reinstatement rights, front or back pay, and the value of lost benefits — but only after first giving the employer written notice identifying the alleged violation and its supporting facts, and then waiting 33 days from that notice for the employer to cure the violation before filing suit. The Labor Commissioner has independent authority to investigate, order temporary relief, issue citations, and sue over violations, and a violation exposes an employer to a $100 civil penalty per affected employee, plus liquidated damages of $100 per employee for each day a violation continues uncured, capped at $1,000 per employee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This part shall not apply to an incumbent grocery employer and the successor grocery employer executing the transfer document with that incumbent grocery employer, if the sum of both of the following is less than 300: (1) The number of grocery workers employed, immediately prior to the change in control, by the incumbent grocery employer across that employer’s grocery establishments nationwide. (2) The number of grocery workers employed, immediately prior to the change in control, by the successor grocery employer across that employer’s grocery establishments nationwide."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2517(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, small-employer (under-300) exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2517.)
  "Parties subject to this part may, by collective bargaining agreement, provide that the agreement supersedes the requirements of this part, in whole or in part, but only if the agreement explicitly sets forth in clear and unambiguous terms the requirements of this part that are superseded."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2512 (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, collective bargaining agreement may supersede the chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2512.)
  "An aggrieved employee or an employee representative, such as a collective bargaining representative or nonprofit corporation, may bring an action in the superior court of the State of California for violations of this part and may be awarded the following:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2510(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, private right of action and recoverable remedies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2510.)
  "Before an employee or an employee representative brings an action in the superior court of the State of California for a violation of this part, both of the following requirements shall be met: (1) The employee has provided written notice to the employer of the provisions of this part alleged to have been violated and the facts to support the alleged violation. (2) The employer has not cured the alleged violation within 33 days from receipt of the written notice."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2510(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, pre-suit written notice and 33-day cure period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2510.)
  "An employer, agent of an employer, or other person who violates this part or causes a violation of this part may be subject to a civil penalty of one hundred dollars ($100) for each employee whose rights under these provisions are violated. An additional amount payable as liquidated damages in the amount of one hundred dollars ($100) per employee, for each day the rights of an employee under this part are violated and continuing until the violation is cured, not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) per employee, which may be recovered by the Labor Commissioner, deposited into the Labor and Workforce Development Fund, and paid to the employee as compensatory damages."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2510(e) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, civil penalty and liquidated damages (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2510.)
  Known gap: The § 2510(a) and § 2510(b) quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 2510) and are not independent of one another. The § 2517 and § 2512 quotes come from separate, independently numbered sections and are independent both of § 2510 and of each other. This clause does not separately quote or otherwise address every scope-limiting provision in the chapter: § 2516 (not quoted here) exempts certain grocery establishments located in long-standing former food deserts, § 2518 (not quoted here) preserves an eligible grocery worker's separate right to sue for wrongful termination, and § 2520 (not quoted here) states that the law does not preempt a local ordinance that offers equal or greater protection — their existence is noted here only so a reader knows to look further if a store's location or a wrongful-termination claim may be relevant. This clause also does not quote § 2510(c)-(d) (the Labor Commissioner's parallel administrative remedies) or § 2510(f)-(j) (citation procedure, injunctive relief, interest, and cumulative-remedies provisions).

CERTIFICATION
The undersigned, Jordan Lee, HR Director of Acme Grocery, Inc., certifies that the transition record above accurately describes, to the best of the undersigned's knowledge, Acme Grocery, Inc.'s actions regarding the retention of eligible grocery workers at the grocery establishment identified above under California's grocery worker retention law, Labor Code §§ 2500-2522.

Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: September 4, 2026

Jordan Lee, HR Director
On behalf of Acme Grocery, Inc.

expectedJSON.body: Retention under the law carries a job-security floor for as long as it lasts, plus a separate check-in point when it ends. During the 90-day transition employment period itself, the successor grocery employer may not discharge a retained eligible grocery worker without cause. At the end of that 90-day period, the successor grocery employer must give each retained eligible grocery worker a written performance evaluation and keep a copy of it for at least three years; if the worker's performance during the 90 days was satisfactory, the successor grocery employer must consider offering the worker continued employment on the terms and conditions the successor grocery employer sets and as otherwise required by law. Separately from the retention and evaluation mechanics, the law includes its own anti-retaliation provision: an employer may not refuse to employ, terminate, reduce the pay of, or otherwise take adverse action against an employee for seeking to enforce rights under the law, including by participating in a proceeding, opposing a practice the law prohibits, or otherwise asserting rights under it — and that protection extends to an employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges the law was not followed.

If the eligible grocery worker’s performance during the 90-day transition employment period is satisfactory, the successor grocery employer shall consider offering the eligible grocery worker continued employment under the terms and conditions established by the successor grocery employer and as required by law. The successor grocery employer shall retain a record of the written performance evaluation for at least three years.

This grocery worker law does not contain equivalent language — § 2506(d) requires only that the successor grocery employer “consider offering” continued employment after a satisfactory 90-day evaluation, and this document did not locate, and does not assume, any provision in §§ 2500-2522 that independently classifies the legal status of employment after the 90-day period ends.

expectedJSON.body: The law's reach has specific limits, and its enforcement runs through both a private right of action and the Labor Commissioner. It does not apply to a change in control where the incumbent and successor grocery employers' combined nationwide grocery-worker headcounts, counted immediately before the change in control, total fewer than 300 — a small-employer exemption that reuses the statute's own “grocery establishment” definition but expands it to include out-of-state stores for purposes of that headcount. Parties covered by the law may also bargain out of some or all of its requirements: a collective bargaining agreement can supersede the law's requirements, but only if the agreement says so explicitly, in clear and unambiguous terms identifying which requirements it replaces. As for enforcement, an aggrieved employee or an employee representative (such as a union or a nonprofit corporation) may sue in superior court for violations and may recover hiring and reinstatement rights, front or back pay, and the value of lost benefits — but only after first giving the employer written notice identifying the alleged violation and its supporting facts, and then waiting 33 days from that notice for the employer to cure the violation before filing suit. The Labor Commissioner has independent authority to investigate, order temporary relief, issue citations, and sue over violations, and a violation exposes an employer to a $100 civil penalty per affected employee, plus liquidated damages of $100 per employee for each day a violation continues uncured, capped at $1,000 per employee.

(2) The number of grocery workers employed, immediately prior to the change in control, by the successor grocery employer across that employer’s grocery establishments nationwide.
